Hurdle and zero-inflated concentration-response models

Source: vignettes/example6.Rmd
example6.Rmd

Overview

In some toxicity tests, exposure can both reduce the response and remove the individual that provides it. For example, a snail exposed to a contaminated sediment may grow more slowly or it may die, and an algal culture may be suppressed or it may fail entirely. The conventional analysis discards the individuals that did not survive and fits a zero-bounded model (e.g. a Gamma) to the remainder.

That analysis is not incorrect, but it answers a narrower question than it appears to. Dropping the individuals that died conditions the estimate on survival, so that it describes growth given that the individual lived, and not growth itself. Because mortality also depends on concentration, the snails that survive a high concentration are a more strongly selected group than those that survive a low one, and these groups are not directly comparable in the way a single fitted curve implies.

A hurdle model retains both processes by splitting the likelihood into a response component, which describes the measurement made on the units that provided one, and a zero-probability component, which describes whether a unit provided a measurement at all. It therefore gives three toxicity estimates where the conventional analysis gives one.

endpoint question in bayesnec
response of survivors how much does exposure suppress growth among individuals that live? which = "growth"
survival how much does exposure kill? which = "survival"
combined what is the expected response per individual exposed? which = "combined" (default)

The combined endpoint is the one the conventional analysis cannot produce. It is generally the quantity of interest for risk assessment, because it is the expected response over the whole exposed cohort, including the individuals that contributed no measurement.

The response and zero-probability components share no parameters. The hurdle log-likelihood is the sum of a term over all individuals and a term over the survivors only,

log p(y_i) = log Bernoulli(alive_i | 1 - hu_i)
           + 1[y_i > 0] * log Gamma(y_i | mu_i, shape)

so with independent priors the posterior factorises. A fit to the survivors only therefore recovers the response component exactly, and is not an approximation to the hurdle model. What such a fit cannot provide is the survival curve or the combined endpoint.

Throughout, the response and zero-probability components are referred to as “growth” and “survival”, after the case these models were written for. Nothing in the implementation is specific to that reading, and any process that produces exact zeros alongside a positive response has this structure (see Other response families for proportions and counts).

To run this vignette we also need

library(bayesnec)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

The nassarius data

The nassarius dataset contains four chronic toxicity tests on the tropical marine snail Nassarius dorsatus (Trenfield et al. 2016), with one row per snail that entered the experiment. A snail that died is recorded with alive = 0 and a growth of zero. The contaminants are anonymised as A–D and the dose units are not stated. Here we use the test of contaminant D, in which 45 of the 372 snails died.

data(nassarius)
snails <- nassarius |>
  filter(contaminant == "D") |>
  select(dose, alive, growth)

Each snail that entered the test must be present in the data, with the dead recorded as zeros. A fit to data from which the dead have been omitted describes a smaller experiment with less mortality. In this test, 36 of the deaths were snails absent from the source records, and were reinstated from the test design (the record column gives the trace of each death; see Deaths recorded by omission).

The doses span more than four orders of magnitude, so we fit the models on a log scale, as in the other vignettes. The control is recorded as a dose of zero, for which the logarithm is undefined, so we add 0.0001 (one decade below the lowest dose tested, 0.001) inside the call to crf(), which is far enough below it to be read as a control and close enough not to stretch the fitted range. Because the transformation is written in the formula, bayesnec returns the estimates and plots on the dose scale (see the Single model usage vignette). The figures below draw dose on this log scale, with the control one decade below the lowest dose.

off <- 1e-4
dose_axis <- scale_x_continuous(
  "Dose", breaks = log(c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10) + off),
  labels = c("0", "0.001", "0.01", "0.1", "1", "10")
)
ggplot(snails, aes(x = log(dose + off), y = growth, colour = alive == 0)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey30", "#eb6834"),
                      labels = c("survived", "died"), name = NULL) +
  dose_axis +
  labs(y = "Growth") +
  theme_classic()

Growth of the snails in the test of contaminant D. A death is recorded as a growth of zero. Points are jittered horizontally.

Growth declines gradually across the series, from a mean of 21.4 in the controls to 14.1 at a dose of 1 and 6.8 at 15, the highest dose at which any snail survived (figure above). Mortality, in contrast, is concentrated at the top of the series. At doses below 10, 6 snails died, spread over 3 doses with no trend with dose, whereas 2 died at 10, 13 of the 24 at 15, and all 24 at 20. These deaths appear as zeros along the bottom of the plot. No survivor has a growth at or below zero (the smallest is 1.9), so the growth of the survivors can be fitted with a Gamma distribution as recorded.

The factorised route

bayesnec provides two ways of fitting a hurdle model. In the factorised route, bnec_hurdle() fits two ordinary bnec() models (a zero-bounded model to the non-zero responses, and a bernoulli model to the survival indicator over all individuals) and returns them together as a bayesnechurdlefit. The combined endpoint is formed afterwards by multiplying the growth and survival posteriors. The joint route, which fits both components as one model, is described in The joint route.

Each component can be given its own equation: crf() names the equation for growth, and model_survival the equation for survival. We begin with one equation for each. Growth declines gradually from the lowest doses and is still declining at 15 (figure above), and we give it the smooth equation ecxll3, a three-parameter log-logistic equation that falls to zero without estimating a lower asymptote. Survival, in contrast, changes little up to a dose of 10 before it falls to zero, and we give it the threshold equation nec3param. A threshold equation for one component and a smooth one for the other also show an NEC and an NSEC side by side (see Endpoints of the factorised fit).

# bayesnec does not set cores; unless mc.cores is set, brms then runs the
# chains one after another. adapt_delta is raised for the reason given below.
fit_f <- bnec_hurdle(
  # Write the offset as 0.001 / 10: brms writes 1e-04 into the Stan program
  # as `1e - 04`, which Stan cannot parse.
  growth ~ crf(log(dose + 0.001 / 10), model = "ecxll3"),
  model_survival = "nec3param", data = snails, seed = 10, refresh = 0,
  cores = 4, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.999)
)

As for any bayesnec fit, the sampler diagnostics should be checked before the estimates are used (see the Multi model usage vignette). check_sampling() returns them for each component.

sampling_f <- check_sampling(fit_f)
sampling_f
#> $growth
#>    model max_rhat  min_ess min_ess_ratio n_divergent failed
#> 1 ecxll3 1.002435 2521.702     0.3152127           0  FALSE
#> 
#> $survival
#>       model max_rhat  min_ess min_ess_ratio n_divergent failed
#> 1 nec3param 1.005095 476.2915    0.05953644          10  FALSE

We raise adapt_delta from its default of 0.8 to 0.999 for all the nassarius fits because of the survival data at the top of the series. Survival changes little from the control to a dose of 10, and then falls to 0.46 at 15 and 0 at 20. Because survival at 15 is about half its control value of 1, these data locate the decline at about 15 but do not limit how steeply it falls: a curve that drops abruptly at 15 fits them about as well as one that falls steadily from 10 to 20. The sampler is therefore likely to have difficulty where it explores those steep curves, and the raised setting reduces the step size it uses there. bnec_hurdle() passes these settings to both components, so growth is fitted with them too. With these settings the growth component produced 0 divergent transitions and the survival component 10, and both components pass every check (table above). The settings can reduce the number of divergent transitions, but they cannot limit the steepness of the decline. That requires a further dose between 10 and 15 or between 15 and 20, or an informative prior on the rate of decline of the survival curve (beta). The other sampler settings, including the 10,000 iterations, are the bayesnec defaults.

Endpoints of the factorised fit

summary() returns the no-effect estimate of each of the three endpoints and, with ecx = TRUE, the ECx at each level in ecx_vals, measured as a percentage decline from the fitted control value (table below). nec(), nsec() and ecx() select one endpoint through their which argument, with the combined endpoint as the default.

summary_f <- summary(fit_f, ecx = TRUE, ecx_vals = c(10, 50))
summary_f
#> Object of class bayesnechurdlefit
#> 
#>    372 individuals exposed; 45 recorded as zero ( 12.1% )
#> 
#>   growth   : Gamma -- ecxll3 
#>   survival : bernoulli -- nec3param 
#> 
#> No-effect toxicity estimates
#>                     Q50  Q2.5 Q97.5
#> combined (N(S)EC)  0.03  0.01  0.09
#> growth (NSEC)      0.03  0.01  0.09
#> survival (NEC)    14.23 10.65 14.94
#> 
#> NSEC values appear where a model set contains smooth (ECx) models, which
#> carry no threshold parameter; N(S)EC is a model-averaged combination
#> of the two (Fisher et al. 2023).
#> 
#> ECx estimates
#>                 Q50  Q2.5 Q97.5
#> combined ec10  0.08  0.03  0.32
#> combined ec50  7.64  5.11 11.10
#> growth ec10    0.08  0.03  0.32
#> growth ec50    7.64  5.11 11.13
#> survival ec10 14.34 10.99 14.94
#> survival ec50 14.90 13.10 15.29
#> 
#> The combined endpoint is the expected response per individual exposed,
#> i.e. growth * survival. Use which = to select a component.
#> 
#> Fitted by bayesnec 2.1.3.44, installed from a local source, which records no commit, under R 4.6.1.

autoplot(fit_f, which = "all") draws the three curves against the recorded dose, on which the ten lowest doses fall within the first twentieth of the width. With x_scale = "fitted", autoplot() instead spaces the curves and the observations on the scale of the fit, log(dose + 0.001 / 10), and labels the axis in dose, including the control at zero. It also marks the no-effect estimate of each endpoint, and with ecx = TRUE the EC10 (figure below).

autoplot(fit_f, which = "all", x_scale = "fitted", ecx = TRUE, xlab = "Dose")

The combined endpoint (response per individual exposed), growth (response of survivors) and survival of the factorised fit, with the median and 95% credible band of each curve. Grey vertical lines mark the no-effect estimate and its credible limits; blue lines mark the EC10 and its limits. The deaths are the zeros along the bottom of the combined panel, and they are absent from the growth panel. The survival panel shows the proportion surviving at each dose.

The growth estimates are between the doses of 0.02 and 10, because growth declines gradually over much of the series, whereas the survival estimates are between 10 and 15, over which survival falls from 0.92 to 0.46 (table and figure above). For example, the EC50 is 7.6 for growth and 15 for survival. On the combined curve, however, the EC10 and EC50 take their growth values (0.083 and 7.6), and the combined curve follows the growth curve up to the survival NEC (14) before it falls to zero with survival. The no-effect estimates are of two kinds, because nec3param estimates a threshold and ecxll3 does not. summary() therefore labels the growth estimate an NSEC (Fisher and Fox 2023), the survival estimate an NEC, and the combined estimate, which is the smaller of the growth and survival estimates in each posterior draw, an N(S)EC (Fisher et al. 2024). The combined estimate (0.035) is close to the growth NSEC (0.035), for the reason given below.

This pattern follows from the definition of the combined curve as the product of the growth and survival curves. Below the dose at which survival begins to fall, survival is at its control value, so the combined curve is a constant multiple of the growth curve. An ECx, which is a percentage decline from the control, is therefore equal on the combined and growth curves up to the dose at which mortality begins, and the growth and combined estimates differ only above that dose. The no-effect estimate that nec() returns with which = "combined" is the per-draw minimum of the growth and survival estimates, and so equals the growth estimate whenever growth is the more sensitive endpoint. This is usually the case, because a contaminant that kills has generally slowed growth at a lower dose first, and it follows from what a threshold is (the dose at which an effect begins): the combined effect begins as soon as either process does.

Above the dose at which survival falls, however, the combined curve drops well below the growth curve, and the difference is largest on the response scale. At a dose of 15, for example, where 11 of the 24 snails survived, the median growth of survivors is 8.8, whereas the expected growth per snail exposed is 3.7. These numbers answer different questions, and which is appropriate depends on whether the assessment concerns the individuals that survive or the population that was exposed.

The practical consequence is that a combined no-effect estimate or low-effect ECx, which will generally be close to the growth estimate, is not a reason to fit a hurdle model. The reasons to fit one are the survival curve, which an analysis of the survivors only cannot produce at all, and the effect sizes at doses where mortality is operating, which such an analysis systematically understates. Where mortality begins before growth has fallen by half, the combined EC50 is also lower than the growth EC50, and The hurdle Beta gives a simulated example constructed that way.

Model averaging

As elsewhere in bayesnec, model averaging is the preferred way of handling uncertainty about the form of the curve (see the Multi model usage vignette), and it is as important for the survival component as for growth. The factorised route makes the full crossed comparison available, in which each growth equation is paired with each survival equation. We fit the "decline" group to both components. model_survival can name a different set for survival, but neither curve is constrained in advance by these data: growth of the survivors is observed only up to a dose of 15, so it may or may not level off above zero, and survival falls to zero, which an equation that estimates a lower asymptote can also describe. bnec() drops three equations of the group from each component: neclin and ecxlin, which are not valid for a Gamma or Bernoulli response under the identity link, and ecxsigm, which it does not fit to a negative predictor such as log(dose + 0.0001).

# The pseudo-BMA weights use a Bayesian bootstrap, which draws from R's random
# number stream.
set.seed(10)

fit_m <- bnec_hurdle(growth ~ crf(log(dose + 0.001 / 10), model = "decline"),
                     model_survival = "decline", data = snails, seed = 10,
                     refresh = 0, cores = 4,
                     control = list(adapt_delta = 0.999))

check_sampling() gives the sampler diagnostics for each equation of the growth and survival sets (table below).

sampling_m <- check_sampling(fit_m)
sampling_m
#> $growth
#>        model max_rhat  min_ess min_ess_ratio n_divergent failed
#> 1  nec3param 1.002629 1823.844     0.2279805           0  FALSE
#> 2  nec4param 1.002323 2032.782     0.2540978           0  FALSE
#> 3     ecxexp 1.001427 3224.339     0.4030424           0  FALSE
#> 4  ecx4param 1.002173 2520.494     0.3150618           0  FALSE
#> 5     ecxwb1 1.001704 1758.125     0.2197656           0  FALSE
#> 6     ecxwb2 1.001461 3002.143     0.3752678           0  FALSE
#> 7   ecxwb1p3 1.001153 1993.339     0.2491674           0  FALSE
#> 8   ecxwb2p3 1.001604 2307.141     0.2883926           0  FALSE

#> 12   ecxflat 1.001778 2548.752     0.3185940           0  FALSE

#>        model max_rhat    min_ess min_ess_ratio n_divergent failed
#> 1  nec3param 1.005095  476.29149   0.059536436          10  FALSE
#> 2  nec4param 1.002213 1112.19432   0.139024290          18   TRUE
#> 3     ecxexp 1.078749   35.33660   0.004417075        6886   TRUE
#> 4  ecx4param 1.002185 1814.41538   0.226801922         911   TRUE
#> 5     ecxwb1 1.001495 1499.57394   0.187446743           9  FALSE
#> 6     ecxwb2 1.003233 1402.65127   0.175331409        1065   TRUE
#> 7   ecxwb1p3 1.013816   51.72488   0.006465610         120   TRUE
#> 8   ecxwb2p3 1.003284 1091.15806   0.136394758        1124   TRUE

#> 10    ecxll4 1.001835  467.40989   0.058426237          23   TRUE

In this fit, none of the 12 growth equations and 8 of the 12 survival equations (nec4param, ecxexp, ecx4param, ecxwb2, ecxwb1p3, ecxwb2p3, ecxll5 and ecxll4) fail at least one check (table above). The survival failures are likely to follow from the design, because the data do not limit how steeply survival falls at 15 (see The factorised route). A combination of a growth and a survival equation should contribute to the model average only where both equations sampled properly. screen_models() applies the thresholds of check_sampling() to each component of a hurdle fit separately, drops from that component each equation that failed, and recomputes the weights of the equations that remain. Because each crossed weight is the product of a growth weight and a survival weight (see below), a combination that includes a dropped equation is removed from the crossed table, which is equivalent to giving it a weight of zero.

set.seed(10)
fit_ms <- screen_models(fit_m)

crossed_weights() gives the weight of each remaining combination (table below). Because the components are independent, the expected log predictive density of a combination is the sum of those of its growth and survival equations, and each crossed weight is the product of a growth weight and a survival weight. The weights of all the combinations therefore follow from the growth and survival fits, without fitting each pair. This identity is specific to pseudo-BMA weights, the bayesnec default, because stacking optimises a different objective whose solution is not in general a product of this kind.

crossed_ms <- crossed_weights(fit_ms)
round(crossed_ms, 2)
#>            survival
#> growth      nec3param ecxwb1 ecxll3 ecxflat
#>   nec3param      0.00   0.00   0.00       0
#>   nec4param      0.00   0.00   0.00       0
#>   ecxexp         0.00   0.00   0.00       0
#>   ecx4param      0.02   0.01   0.02       0
#>   ecxwb1         0.05   0.02   0.07       0
#>   ecxwb2         0.01   0.00   0.01       0
#>   ecxwb1p3       0.19   0.09   0.26       0
#>   ecxwb2p3       0.01   0.00   0.01       0
#>   ecxll5         0.01   0.01   0.02       0
#>   ecxll4         0.02   0.01   0.03       0
#>   ecxll3         0.05   0.02   0.06       0
#>   ecxflat        0.00   0.00   0.00       0

No growth equation failed a check, so screen_models() returns the growth weights unchanged. Before screening, the survival equations that failed a check were given 0.62 of the survival weight, and screen_models() drops them from the average. After screening, 4 survival equations remain, and the weight is spread across their combinations with the growth equations. Of the growth weight after screening, 0.54 is given to ecxwb1p3 and less than 0.01 to the threshold equations (nec3param and nec4param) (table above). The model average is compared with a single combination in Refitting a selected combination.

Each model set includes smooth (ECx) equations as well as threshold equations. The ECx estimates compared in Refitting a selected combination are read off the model-averaged curves, as for a single equation. The no-effect estimate that summary() and nec() report for such a set is a weighted mixture of NEC and NSEC draws. A smooth equation has no threshold parameter, so its contribution to that estimate is an NSEC (Fisher and Fox 2023), not an NEC, and bayesnec refers to the mixture as the N(S)EC (Fisher et al. 2024). summary() labels each endpoint accordingly, whereas nec() returns the estimate as an unlabelled vector with a message to that effect, so summary() is the better choice where the distinction is important.

autoplot() draws the model-averaged curves of the screened sets with the arguments used for the single factorised fit (figure below). bayesnec forms each averaged curve from the posterior draws of the equations in its set, taken in proportion to their weights, so its credible band includes the uncertainty about the form of the curve as well as that about the parameters of each equation.

autoplot(fit_ms, which = "all", x_scale = "fitted", ecx = TRUE, xlab = "Dose")

The model-averaged combined endpoint (response per individual exposed), growth (response of survivors) and survival of the screened sets, with the median and 95% credible band of each curve. Grey vertical lines mark the no-effect estimate and its credible limits; blue lines mark the EC10 and its limits. Points are the growth of each snail in the combined panel, with the deaths as zeros, the growth of the survivors in the growth panel, and the proportion surviving at each dose in the survival panel.

On the growth panel, the no-effect estimate of the average is an N(S)EC of 0.034 (0.0085–0.10), close to the NSEC of ecxll3 in the single factorised fit, 0.035 (0.0077–0.092). On the survival panel, 0.64 of the weight is given to smooth equations, whose contribution to the no-effect estimate is an NSEC, so the survival no-effect estimate of the average is an N(S)EC of 13 (7.3–15). This is below the NEC of nec3param in the single factorised fit, 14 (11–15), and its interval is 1.8 times as wide. The combined no-effect estimate of the average is an N(S)EC of 0.034 (0.0062–0.10), close to its growth estimate.

The joint route

In the joint route, bnec(family = "hurdle_gamma") fits one model with two parameter blocks. brms names the second block hu (or zi for the zero-inflated families), and bayesnec gives that block its own concentration-response curve, with the block name as a prefix on each of its non-linear parameters (e.g. top belongs to the response block and hutop to the survival block). Because the likelihood factorises, the factorised and joint routes give equivalent inference, so the choice between them depends on what each can fit.

factorised (bnec_hurdle) joint (family = "hurdle_gamma")
different equation on each block yes, via model_survival yes, via model_survival
model averaging full crossed set via crossed_weights() response block only
coupling the blocks (e.g. shared group-level effect) no — breaks the factorisation yes
number of fits two one

We recommend the factorised route by default, because it makes the crossed model comparison tractable. The joint route is needed where the growth and survival blocks must share structure (e.g. a group-level effect common to both), which the factorisation cannot express. The routes are intended to be used in sequence: the model sets are fitted with bnec_hurdle(), screened with screen_models() and averaged, a combination is selected from crossed_weights(), and bnec_joint() refits that combination jointly, with whatever shared structure is required.

Survival in the second block

Both routes model the probability of surviving, which declines with dose, but they arrive at it in different ways. In the factorised route the second fit has a response of its own: bnec_hurdle() constructs an alive/dead indicator (1 for alive) and fits an ordinary bernoulli model to it, so nothing is inverted. In the joint route, however, hu is a distributional parameter of the response itself, and brms defines it as the probability of a zero (i.e. mortality). This definition belongs to the family and cannot be exchanged for its complement, so bayesnec writes

hu = 1 - (an ordinary bayesnec equation, parameters prefixed)

so that the equation describes the declining survival curve of the factorised route, while hu keeps the meaning brms requires. The 1 - makes the joint route agree with the factorised route, and does not represent a modelling decision.

Placing the declining curve on survival has three consequences. First, all 24 equations are available for the second block unchanged. beta is exponentiated in each equation that includes it, so the equations can only decline (or, for ecxflat, stay constant), and none of them can express an increasing mortality curve. Second, hutop is the control survival, which is near 1, so it takes the prior a bernoulli fit would use, whereas the equivalent mortality parameter would lie near its lower bound of 0, where it samples poorly. Third, ecx() and nsec() apply unchanged. Both require a declining curve, and both invert the zero-probability block to survival before computing, so an EC10 has the meaning here that it has for any other model in the package. Nothing is lost in exchange, because hunec, the dose at which survival begins to fall, is also the dose at which mortality begins to rise. When reading output, note that hutop and hunec describe survival (e.g. a hutop near 1 indicates near-complete survival in the controls).

Refitting a selected combination

Model averaging is done on the factorised fit, because the joint route can average over the response block only. Where a single fit is required, best_crossed() identifies the combination with the largest crossed weight, and bnec_joint() refits a combination as one two-block model, by default the one best_crossed() selects. We apply both to the screened sets, so that the selected combination is one whose growth and survival equations both sampled properly.

best <- best_crossed(fit_ms)
best
#> $growth
#> [1] "ecxwb1p3"
#> 
#> $survival
#> [1] "ecxll3"
#> 
#> $weight
#> [1] 0.2554268

Here the combination with the largest weight is ecxwb1p3 growth with ecxll3 survival (0.26).

fit_j <- bnec_joint(fit_ms, seed = 10, refresh = 0, cores = 4,
                    control = list(adapt_delta = 0.999))

pull_best() returns the factorised fit of this combination from the screened sets, without refitting, so the factorised and joint routes can be compared on one pair of equations. We compare their EC10 for each endpoint with that of the model average (table below). A factorised fit selects an endpoint through the which argument, and a joint fit through dpar, which names the brms distributional parameter: "mu" for growth, "hu" for survival, and the default NULL for the combined endpoint. These arguments are not interchangeable, so where a component estimate looks like the combined one, it is useful to check class(fit). Note also that the no-effect estimate of a joint fit is the combined one, with no argument for selecting a block: nsec() returns it for any pair of equations, whereas nec() requires a growth equation with an nec parameter.

fit_b <- pull_best(fit_ms)

ec10 <- rbind(
  `growth, factorised` = ecx(fit_b, which = "growth"),
  `growth, joint` = ecx(fit_j, dpar = "mu"),
  `growth, model average` = ecx(fit_ms, which = "growth"),
  `survival, factorised` = ecx(fit_b, which = "survival"),
  `survival, joint` = ecx(fit_j, dpar = "hu"),
  `survival, model average` = ecx(fit_ms, which = "survival"),
  `combined, factorised` = ecx(fit_b),
  `combined, joint` = ecx(fit_j),
  `combined, model average` = ecx(fit_ms)
)
signif(ec10, 2)
#>                            Q50  Q2.5 Q97.5
#> growth, factorised       0.070 0.028  0.28
#> growth, joint            0.072 0.027  0.28
#> growth, model average    0.077 0.028  0.32
#> survival, factorised    13.000 9.900 15.00
#> survival, joint         13.000 9.700 15.00
#> survival, model average 13.000 9.700 15.00
#> combined, factorised     0.070 0.028  0.28
#> combined, joint          0.072 0.027  0.28
#> combined, model average  0.077 0.028  0.32

The EC10 medians of the factorised and joint fits of the selected combination differ by at most 2.6% across the three endpoints (table above). Both routes fit the equations with identical likelihoods and priors, so they estimate one posterior, and the difference is therefore likely to reflect Monte Carlo error. The joint fit produced 1 divergent transition and passes the checks of check_sampling(), as both of its equations did in the factorised fit. These results suggest that the factorised and joint routes differ in the models they can fit, and not in the estimates they give for a model both can fit.

autoplot() takes the same which argument for a joint fit as for a factorised one, so the joint refit is drawn as the factorised pair was (figure below).

autoplot(fit_j, which = "all", x_scale = "fitted", ecx = TRUE, xlab = "Dose",
         point_alpha = 0.25)

The combined endpoint (response per individual exposed), growth (response of survivors) and survival of the joint refit, with the median and 95% credible band of each curve. Grey vertical lines mark the no-effect estimate of each panel and its credible limits; blue lines mark the EC10 and its limits. Points are as in the figure of the model average.

On the combined panel the grey lines mark the combined NSEC of the joint refit, 0.038 (0.012–0.097), and the blue lines its combined EC10, and the EC10 of each block is in the table above. At a dose of 15, where survival has fallen to about half its control value, the median expected growth per snail exposed is 3.5 for the joint refit and 3.6 for the model average (figure in Model averaging), against 3.7 for the single factorised fit of ecxll3 with nec3param (figure in Endpoints of the factorised fit). At this dose, selecting one combination therefore changes the combined response little from that of the model average.

The model average gives a growth EC10 of 0.077 (0.028–0.32), against 0.070 (0.028–0.28) for the selected combination alone (table above). The interval of the model average is wider than that of the selected combination, which is likely to reflect the 0.46 of the growth weight given to equations other than ecxwb1p3, whose curves may begin to decline at different doses.

The equation for each block is set independently, so a joint fit with any combination can also be requested directly, with crf() naming the equation for the response block and model_survival the equation for the survival block. bnec_joint() is a convenience wrapper that fills in these names from best_crossed() where they are not given.

bnec(growth ~ crf(log(dose + 0.001 / 10), model = "ecxll3"), data = snails,
     family = "hurdle_gamma", model_survival = "nec3param")

Selecting a single combination discards the rest of the crossed table, which is a substantial loss of information where the weights are spread across several combinations. This step is therefore justified only where the joint form is needed for a reason the factorisation cannot accommodate. The main such reason is group-level structure spanning both blocks, which is supplied through the formula argument of bnec_joint().

Other response families

Count responses

A structural zero in a count response uses hurdle_poisson or hurdle_negbinomial, not the similarly named zero-inflated family. A hurdle states that every zero came from the survival process. Its positive-count likelihood is therefore conditional on Y > 0, and the two blocks factorise. bnec_hurdle() applies trunc(lb = 1) internally to the growth fit, while the joint hurdle families include the same normalisation in their density.

zero_inflated_poisson and zero_inflated_negbinomial apply where the source of a zero is unknown. An observed zero can then arise from either the count distribution or the added zero-probability component. The likelihood contains both possibilities in one mixture term and cannot be fitted as two independent models. bayesnec fits the concentration-response curve to the count mean and holds the zero-inflation probability constant for these families.

For count hurdles, the response of survivors is E[Y | Y > 0]. bayesnec computes that quantity exactly from the truncated growth fit’s underlying count parameters. This avoids the finite upper grid that brms uses for expected predictions from a general truncated discrete model, which can omit a substantial negative-binomial tail. For a joint count hurdle, ecx(dpar = "mu") and nsec(dpar = "mu") convert the underlying Poisson or negative-binomial mean to the same conditional mean. The fitted top and bot parameters of the joint equation remain on the underlying count-mean scale.

The factorised count route requires brms 2.23.2 or later. Earlier brms versions used a different lower-bound convention in log_lik(), so bnec_hurdle() refuses the route before fitting and points to the corresponding joint hurdle family.

The hurdle Beta

zero_inflated_beta is the direct analogue of hurdle_gamma for a proportional response bounded on (0, 1), with a Beta response block for the units that gave a measurement and a survival block for whether a unit gave one at all. It applies where a proportion is measured on each unit and some units fail entirely, for example an algal culture expressed as a proportion of a design ceiling, with replicates that crashed.

A zero-inflated Gamma or Beta model is identical to the corresponding hurdle model. Zero-inflation differs from a hurdle only where the base distribution can itself produce zeros, which the Gamma and Beta distributions cannot. Consistent with this, the Stan density that brms generates for zero_inflated_beta is the hurdle form, with no mixture at zero. bayesnec treats the zero-inflated and hurdle forms identically and keeps the brms name, so hurdle_gamma and zero_inflated_beta differ in name and in the support of the response, but not in structure.

In practice, however, the conditions under which this family is appropriate are more restrictive than they first appear, and the most likely misuse is to choose it simply because a proportion contains some zeros.

Conditions for a hurdle Beta

A hurdle Beta is appropriate only where all of the following conditions are met:

  • the proportion has a denominator that is fixed by design or measured per unit, and is not a control mean or an observed maximum (see Unavoidable divisors in the Single model usage vignette);
  • the response declines, matching the convention of the bayesnec model set;
  • the zeros are structural, produced by a process that genuinely fails; and
  • there is no mass at 1.

The last condition is the one that limits use of the family in practice, and it fails for structural reasons, not by accident:

  • if the denominator is the unit’s own baseline, the response can exceed it and produce values at or above 1, and capping these at 1 converts the excess into a spike at the boundary (i.e. flooring, discussed below, applied at the other end of the scale);
  • if the “nothing happened” state is at the top of the scale, the inflation is at 1 and not at 0, which requires a different family; and
  • if the response is genuinely a count out of a known total, the binomial is already correct and no Beta is needed.

A response inflated at both boundaries requires zero_one_inflated_beta or an ordered-Beta treatment, and these are not available in bayesnec. A response that is a ratio to a per-unit baseline is often better modelled with hurdle_gamma on the uncapped ratio.

A simulated example

No dataset shipped with bayesnec satisfies all four conditions, nor did any of the candidates considered while this vignette was written, and the mass-at-1 condition is the one that failed, for the structural reasons given above. The example below is therefore simulated, and constructed to meet all four conditions. It shows what the family does where it applies, and it is not evidence that any particular real dataset qualifies, so the conditions above should still be checked before the family is used.

The scenario is an algal growth-rate test. Growth is expressed as a proportion of a ceiling fixed in advance by the test protocol (i.e. not a control mean and not the observed maximum, as the first condition requires). A culture that crashes contributes an exact zero, and a culture that grows contributes a proportion drawn from a Beta distribution, which cannot itself return a zero, so each zero in the data is structural. The concentrations are a twofold dilution series with a control (0 and 1 to 64), and we generate and fit both curves on log(x + 1), on which the series is close to evenly spaced. An offset of one is reasonable here because one is the lowest concentration tested, and it places the control one step below it.

set.seed(101)

nec3 <- function(x, top, beta, nec) {
  top * exp(-exp(beta) * (x - nec) * (x > nec))
}

# Growth declines gradually from a control proportion of 0.70, with a threshold
# at a concentration of 3. Every culture grows up to a concentration of 6, above
# which they crash in increasing numbers, before growth has fallen by half.
growth_true <- function(x) {
  nec3(log(x + 1), top = 0.70, beta = log(0.37), nec = log(3 + 1))
}
survival_true <- function(x) {
  nec3(log(x + 1), top = 1, beta = log(0.7), nec = log(6 + 1))
}

conc <- rep(c(0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64), each = 16)
alive <- rbinom(length(conc), 1, survival_true(conc))
# 30 is the Beta precision: higher values give tighter scatter about mu.
prop <- rbeta(length(conc), growth_true(conc) * 30,
              (1 - growth_true(conc)) * 30)

zib_dat <- data.frame(x = conc, y = ifelse(alive == 1, prop, 0))

Two of the conditions can be checked directly from the data: that there is no mass at 1, and that the zeros are confined to crashed cultures, not small measurements.

c(n = nrow(zib_dat),
  zeros = sum(zib_dat$y == 0),
  max = round(max(zib_dat$y), 3),
  at_or_above_1 = sum(zib_dat$y >= 1))
#>             n         zeros           max at_or_above_1 
#>       128.000        33.000         0.877         0.000

table(dose = zib_dat$x, measured = zib_dat$y > 0)
#>     measured
#> dose FALSE TRUE
#>   0      0   16
#>   1      0   16
#>   2      0   16
#>   4      0   16
#>   8      2   14
#>   16     7    9
#>   32    11    5
#>   64    13    3

The largest observed proportion is 0.88 and no value is at or above 1, so there is no spike at the boundary for the Beta to accommodate. Cultures crash at the top four concentrations, in increasing numbers instead of all at once, and at least 3 of the 16 grew at every concentration, which leaves the response block with data at each dose and the survival threshold identifiable (table above).

bnec_hurdle() takes the data unchanged. It selects the response family from the non-zero rows, and so chooses a Beta here, where it chose a Gamma for the snail growth. The joint route would instead name the family, as family = "zero_inflated_beta", and its second block is named zi, not hu, so the survival parameters appear as zitop, zibeta and zinec.

zib_f <- bnec_hurdle(y ~ crf(log(x + 1), model = "nec3param"),
                     data = zib_dat, seed = 101, refresh = 0)
# The generating EC50 is the concentration at which a generating curve falls to
# half its value at the control. The combined curve is growth times survival.
ec50_true <- function(f) uniroot(function(x) f(x) - f(0) / 2, c(0, 64))$root
generating <- c(3, 6, 3, ec50_true(growth_true), ec50_true(survival_true),
                ec50_true(function(x) growth_true(x) * survival_true(x)))
zib_est <- rbind(
  `growth nec` = nec(zib_f, which = "growth"),
  `survival nec` = nec(zib_f, which = "survival"),
  `combined nec` = nec(zib_f),
  `growth ec50` = ecx(zib_f, which = "growth", ecx_val = 50),
  `survival ec50` = ecx(zib_f, which = "survival", ecx_val = 50),
  `combined ec50` = ecx(zib_f, ecx_val = 50)
)
data.frame(generating = signif(generating, 3), signif(zib_est, 3))
#>               generating   Q50  Q2.5 Q97.5
#> growth nec           3.0  1.93  1.15  2.98
#> survival nec         6.0  6.44  3.71 11.80
#> combined nec         3.0  1.93  1.15  2.97
#> growth ec50         25.0 28.00 19.70 45.90
#> survival ec50       17.8 19.20 13.40 32.00
#> combined ec50       10.0 10.30  7.94 14.30

The combined no-effect estimate is the per-draw minimum of the growth and survival NECs, so its generating value is the smaller threshold, 3. Each generating value lies inside its 95% credible interval except that of the growth NEC and the combined no-effect estimate (table above). In this simulated data set the mean of the cultures that grew is 0.73 at the control and 0.69 at a concentration of 2, whereas the generating curve is at 0.70 for both, so the data decline from below the generating threshold, and the growth NEC is estimated below it. The precision of the thresholds is limited by the design, not by the family. A threshold model can locate a change point only as sharply as the dose spacing around it allows. The generating growth threshold of 3 falls in the gap between the doses at 2 and 4, and the survival threshold of 6 in the gap between 4 and 8, and with nothing observed inside a gap the likelihood is nearly flat across it. The survival NEC, 6.4 (3.7–12), is the less precise of the two, because each culture contributes only whether it grew. Where a threshold is the quantity of interest, placing doses around it is therefore likely to narrow its interval more than extra replication elsewhere.

The EC50 is where survival changes the combined estimate. Growth declines gradually from a concentration of 3 and has fallen by half only at about 25, whereas the cultures begin to crash above 6. At the concentration at which growth has halved, only 40 per cent of cultures grow at all, so the combined curve falls to half its control value at a lower concentration: the combined EC50 is 10 (7.9–14), against 28 (20–46) for growth and 19 (13–32) for survival (table above). The combined no-effect estimate, 1.9 (1.1–3.0), is in contrast equal to the growth NEC, because growth begins to decline at a lower concentration than survival, as it did for the snails.

autoplot() draws the three curves of the factorised fit (figure below), and with ecx = TRUE and ecx_val = 50 it marks the EC50 of each panel beside the no-effect estimate it draws by default. On the log1p axis, which is log(x + 1) and so the scale of the fit, the control and the doses of the series are spaced as they were fitted. The combined curve follows the growth curve up to the survival NEC, and above it falls further than growth as the cultures crash. At 64, for example, the median proportion achieved by cultures that grew is 0.28, whereas the expected proportion per culture started is 0.058.

autoplot(zib_f, which = "all", ecx = TRUE, ecx_val = 50,
         xlab = "Concentration") +
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "log1p",
                     breaks = c(0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64))

The simulated hurdle Beta. The combined endpoint (response per individual exposed) is the expected proportion per culture started, growth (response of survivors) the proportion achieved by cultures that grew, and survival the probability of a culture growing at all. Grey vertical lines mark the NEC of each panel and its credible limits (on the combined panel, the per-draw minimum of the growth and survival NECs), and blue lines the EC50 and its limits. Concentration is drawn on a log(x + 1) axis, the scale of the fit.

The origin of the zeros

A hurdle model assumes that each zero is structural, i.e. that it marks a unit that died or failed. A zero in concentration-response data can instead be a value rounded down at the recording resolution, a negative value replaced by zero, or a genuine measurement near zero. Conversely, a death can be recorded by leaving the unit out of the data, so that the zero it should contribute is missing. The subsections below describe how to recognise each case.

Zeros from rounding

bayesnec ships the herbicide dataset (Jones and Kerswell 2003), which contains 23 zero values in fvfm (maximum quantum yield). These zeros appear to make the data candidates for zero-inflation. However, they are not, and fitting zero_inflated_beta to them would be misleading.

data(herbicide)

herbicide |>
  group_by(herbicide) |>
  summarise(n = n(), zeros = sum(fvfm == 0),
            min_nonzero = min(fvfm[fvfm > 0]), .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 7 × 4
#>   herbicide       n zeros min_nonzero
#>   <chr>       <int> <int>       <dbl>
#> 1 ametryn        96    12        0.01
#> 2 atrazine       84     0        0.04
#> 3 diuron         72     0        0.02
#> 4 hexazinone     76     1        0.01
#> 5 irgarol        72    10        0.01
#> 6 simazine       72     0        0.16
#> 7 tebuthiuron   108     0        0.04

Two features of the data indicate the origin of these zeros. First, each value is a multiple of the recording resolution, and the smallest non-zero value is equal to one unit of that resolution.

nonzero <- herbicide$fvfm[herbicide$fvfm > 0]
c(resolution = min(diff(sort(unique(nonzero)))),
  smallest_nonzero = min(nonzero))
#>       resolution smallest_nonzero 
#>             0.01             0.01

A recorded 0.00 therefore means that the true value was below 0.005. It does not mark a distinct event, but a measurement that was rounded down.

Second, the zeros appear only where the curve falls below the rounding floor (0.005). Diuron has no zeros, and its means decline smoothly and level off above the floor (0.043 at the highest concentration, 30), whereas zeros appear only for the more potent compounds (ametryn, hexazinone and irgarol), whose curves go lower. Diuron was tested with the organisms and the instrument used for the other herbicides, and yet its data contain no zeros.

herbicide |>
  filter(herbicide == "diuron") |>
  group_by(concentration) |>
  summarise(mean_fvfm = round(mean(fvfm), 3), .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   concentration mean_fvfm
#>           <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1           0.1     0.698
#> 2           0.3     0.639
#> 3           1       0.491
#> 4           3       0.27 
#> 5          10       0.092
#> 6          30       0.043

Fitting a hurdle model to these data would give the zi block its own NEC and ECx for the probability of rounding to zero, which is a measurement artefact and not an endpoint. In addition, the mu block would be biased upward at high concentrations, because conditioning on y > 0 truncates precisely the smallest values.

Each of these zeros is instead a value known only to lie in [0, 0.005), i.e. a censored observation (see the Censoring section of vignette("example1")). The default bayesnec behaviour of nudging zeros to min(y[y > 0]) / 10 is crude, but defensible in this case, because 0.001 falls inside the true interval. The herbicide fits of vignette("example4") treat these zeros as left-censored at 0.005 instead.

The diagnostic for this case is a comparison of the gap between zero and the smallest non-zero value against the resolution the data were recorded at. Where the gap is much greater than the resolution, the zeros mark a distinct process and a hurdle model applies. Where the gap is approximately equal to the resolution, the zeros are rounding or censoring, and a hurdle model does not apply.

gap_ratio <- function(y) {
  y <- y[!is.na(y)]
  nonzero <- y[y > 0]
  resolution <- min(diff(sort(unique(nonzero))))
  min(nonzero) / resolution
}

c(herbicide = gap_ratio(herbicide$fvfm),
  simulated = gap_ratio(zib_dat$y))
#> herbicide simulated 
#>       1.0  125523.1

A ratio near 1 (as for herbicide) indicates that the smallest non-zero value is one rounding unit above zero, so zero is simply the next value down. A large ratio (about 125,520 for the simulated hurdle Beta data) indicates a real gap between “no response” and “the smallest response that was measured”.

Zeros from flooring

The gap diagnostic tests whether the zeros are separated from the continuum of measured values. It does not test how many causes the zeros have, and no test computed on the processed data can do so. This is the second thing to establish, and it is a question of provenance (i.e. how the data were recorded and prepared), not of computation.

state true value kind of zero
individual died / replicate failed undefined structural
individual shrank / population declined negative floored — a substituted value
no measurable change ≈ 0 genuine

A hurdle model assumes structural zeros. Growth endpoints, however, frequently contain floored zeros, because negative growth rates, yields or increments are routinely replaced with 0, or nudged to a small positive value, so that a zero-bounded family will accept them. Three things go wrong at once when a floored response is analysed:

  1. a living, measured individual is assigned to the state of a dead one;
  2. the response block conditions on y > 0, so the “response of survivors” silently becomes the “response of those that happened to increase”, which is selection on the outcome, and because decline is concentration-dependent this bias grows with dose; and
  3. the zero-probability block then mixes failure with decline, and describes neither.

The biases in the response and zero-probability blocks run in one direction and both increase with dose, so the fitted curves for these blocks are pulled apart precisely where the toxicological signal is strongest.

Flooring is substitution at a boundary, and the case against substitution is well established: it fabricates data, biases statistics and obscures real relationships (Helsel 2006). Establishing which kind of zero is present before choosing a model is standard advice (Blasco-Moreno et al. 2019; Martin et al. 2005), as is the warning that many zeros do not by themselves indicate zero inflation (Warton 2005).

The regulatory standard also advises against substitution, and for the same reason. OECD TG 201 (OECD 2026) defines growth endpoints that admit negative values, namely the average specific growth rate, µ = (ln X_j − ln X_i)/(t_j − t_i) (eq. 1, ¶49), and the yield (the biomass at the end of the test minus the biomass at the start, ¶53). Annex 5 is explicit about values that fall outside the expected range, stating both what to do with them and what not to do:

Negative inhibitions may be a problem with for instance the log-normal distribution function likewise demanding an alternative regression function. It is not recommended to assign a zero or small positive value to such negative values because this distorts the error distribution.

These sentences concern negative inhibition (growth stimulation at low concentrations), not negative growth rates, so they are not a ruling on this case. However, the reason and the remedy are both general, and both apply here: change the function, not the values.

The meaning of “distorts the error distribution”

The phrase is precise, and not rhetorical. Write µ(x) for the fitted mean at concentration x, σ for the residual scale and f for the density. For a unit whose growth was measured as some negative value y, keeping the value and flooring it contribute differently to the likelihood:

treatment contribution what it asserts
keep y, on a real-line scale f(y; µ(x), σ) the true value is y — true
floor to zero f(0; µ(x), σ) the true value is 0 — false

The first row is the remedy the guideline points to (i.e. keep the value, and choose a regression function able to accommodate it). Its contribution is largest when µ(x) is near y, so the fitted curve is free to follow the data down. Flooring (the second row) replaces this with a contribution that is largest when µ(x) is near zero, so each floored observation pulls the curve up toward zero. Because floored values cluster at the top of the concentration range, that pull is concentrated precisely where the response is changing fastest, and the result is a fit biased upward in a dose-dependent way. This is what distorting the error distribution amounts to in practice.

The three failures listed above for a floored response all follow from the way a hurdle model allocates observations between its two blocks. This bias, in contrast, originates in the likelihood contribution of the substituted value itself, and is therefore present in an ordinary regression that has no zero-probability block at all. Fitting a simpler model does not avoid it.

The provenance question

Can this endpoint take negative values in principle? Rates, increments, differences and yields all can. If it can, and the data as supplied contain zeros but no negative values, the zeros should not be accepted as structural until it has been established how negative values were handled, either from the raw measurements or from whoever prepared the data.

In the nassarius data, for example, growth can be negative in principle, and 4 survivors across the four tests are recorded with a negative growth, which indicates that negative values were not floored upstream and that the zeros are deaths. Zeros of different origin cannot be distinguished once written to file. The gap test and the provenance question are complementary: the gap test asks whether the zeros are distinct from the continuum, and the provenance question asks whether they are distinct from each other.

Recommended handling

We recommend two ways of handling a growth endpoint that can fall below zero, depending on what the assessment requires:

  1. Where the values were measured and can be kept, do not floor them. Model the response on a scale that admits them, with a family on the real line.
  2. Where a strictly positive scale is required, model the response relative to each unit’s own baseline.

The first recommendation keeps the values as measured (e.g. a specific growth rate, or the raw increment), and uses an equation with a lower asymptote (e.g. nec4param or ecx4param) so that the curve can cross zero. On a Gaussian response bayesnec also fits the zero-bounded equations, whose curves cannot fall below zero, and the model weights then assess that shape against the data. Any hurdle should be driven by the recorded failure indicator, not by y == 0.

Under the second recommendation the only zeros are genuine failures, and hurdle_gamma is correct. Note that the ECx must then be defined on the derived increment, because a 50% reduction in a ratio and a 50% reduction in the increment are different quantities, and can differ by more than an order of magnitude.

Deaths recorded by omission

Deaths are often recorded by omission or by a sentinel code, not as zeros, and must be reconstructed before fitting. bnec_hurdle() requires each unit that entered the experiment to be present in the data, with 0 recorded for those that gave no response. Rows omitted, instead of recorded as zero, cannot be distinguished from rows that were never run, and would be read as a smaller experiment instead of as additional zeros.

Common traces to look for include:

  • sentinel codes, often one constant per test run, well below the real data (a large gap between the sentinel and the next real value makes these unambiguous);
  • blank replicates within a tank or plate that is present;
  • absent tanks or plates within a treatment that is present, where the whole unit failed; and
  • an omitted top concentration, where all units died and the treatment does not appear in the file.

The last of these is the easiest to miss and has the greatest consequence where the omitted concentration is the lowest one at which all units died, because the information about where survival collapses comes from the doses between the last with full survival and the first with none. Concentrations above that one, at which all units also died, are likely to change the survival estimates much less. The test of contaminant D is an example: all 24 snails at a dose of 20 are absent from the source records, and without them the data would end at 15, where 11 of the 24 snails survived.
